Surgical Breast Enlargement

Breast Implant Rippling and Visibility: Causes and Prevention

Rippling means wave-like ridges or wrinkles that can be seen or felt at the edges of an implant. It is a recognised issue, not a sign that you did something wrong.

Home/Surgical Breast Enlargement/Breast Implant Rippling and Visibility: Causes and Prevention

Visible or palpable rippling is one of the more common cosmetic concerns after augmentation. It is more likely in some bodies and with some implant choices than others.

Why it happens

  • Thin tissue coverage: little natural breast tissue or fat over the implant.
  • Implant position: implants placed over the muscle tend to show more.
  • Implant type: saline implants are generally more prone than cohesive silicone gel, though not exclusively.
  • Underfilling: a saline implant filled below its recommended volume can fold.
  • Size: an implant that is large relative to your tissue.
  • Weight loss or ageing: reducing the cover over time.

Where it shows

Rippling is most often noticed on the sides and lower part of the breast, and when leaning forward or standing. It may be felt rather than seen.

Reducing the risk

  • Choose an implant volume that suits your tissue.
  • Discuss placement under the muscle if you have little coverage; see implant placement.
  • Talk about the pros and cons of saline versus silicone for you.
  • Consider adding fat transfer on top of the implant in selected cases, as some surgeons do.
  • Maintain a stable weight.

If you are very lean or have little breast tissue, discuss whether implants are the right option at all. Fat transfer or a different approach may be more suitable in selected cases.

When rippling needs medical review

Rippling alone is usually cosmetic, but a new ridge with pain, a change in shape or a lump should be assessed. If the implant feels different or the breast becomes firm, your surgeon may check for rupture or capsular contracture. Do not assume every new change is rippling.

What if it develops?

Mild rippling may be acceptable. If it bothers you, options include changing the implant, adjusting placement or adding soft-tissue cover. Each has trade-offs and should be discussed with a surgeon. See breast revision. Revision is not guaranteed to remove rippling completely, especially if your tissue is thin, so ask what improvement is realistic before agreeing to another operation.

Questions to ask

  • How likely is visible rippling in someone with my tissue?
  • Which choice reduces it for me?
  • What would you do if it occurs?

Key takeaway

Honest assessment of your tissue before surgery is the best protection against visible implants. See the breast implants guide.

Draft review and sources

Before publication: qualified clinician review and current Indian regulatory verification, where relevant, are required. Sources: FDA: Breast Implants · CDSCO: Medical Device & Diagnostics.
